newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU harmonisation seen cutting Dutch inflation rate.
newsitem.headline: EU harmonisation seen cutting Dutch inflation rate.

text.p: EU-harmonised consumer price data will lead to a lower Dutch inflation figure than that based on the traditional Dutch method, analysts said on Wednesday.
The harmonised consumer price index (CPI), due to be published for the first time on Friday, is meant to provide a better comparison of inflation among EU states.

The Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) said on Wednesday the EU harmonised data stripped out certain items included in the domestic CPI: imputed rents on owner-occupied homes; consumption-linked taxes; club membership and college fees; package holidays; some types of insurance and other costs.

"Consumer-linked taxes and rents have risen relatively fast recently. So have expenses abroad, contributions and college fees over the last couple of years, be it in a somewhat lesser extent," said Frank Heemskerk, analyst at ABN Amro.
"Taking these out, does make quite a difference, especially as Germany does not include rents in its CPI," he said.

ING analyst Fred Pallada expected the rise in the harmonised CPI in February to be one percentage point below the traditional CPI on an annual basis. "We count on a rise in the EU-harmonised figure for February of 1.5 percent (on an annual basis) while we estimate the old CPI at plus 2.5 percent," he said.
He added that on a monthly basis, he expected traditional CPI to have increased by 0.5 percent in February, versus a 0.7 percent increase in the harmonised figure.
"The year-on-year figure includes rents and taxes, which are generally hiked in January, leading to a higher traditional index," he said.

"The higher EU estimate on a monthly basis should be attributed to the introduction of new, more expensive collections of clothes, which is felt stronger in the EU figure due to the different weighting," Pallada said.
A Reuters poll has shown Dutch analysts expect the traditional February CPI to have risen 2.4 percent on an annual basis, and 0.4 percent on a monthly basis.

The harmonised rate, which will be used to judge which EU members meet inflation criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU), will be published alongside existing consumer price index (CPI) data.
The harmonised index will use 1996 as the base year (index at 100) while the traditional measure uses 1990, but both use 1990 consumption patterns.

Rabobank International said in its latest Financial Weekly report that it expected the harmonised figure would not differ too much from the interim harmonised index, which European statistics agencies have been calculating since January 1996.
It said the interim harmonised CPI figure for December was 1.9 percent, against the traditional measure of 2.5 percent.
